Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip WFP is committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is guided by a strategic, programmatic and governance instrument to operationalize its plan and achieve its project objectives to: 
• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity. 
WFP’s interventions focus on high food insecurity levels, including the malnutrition levels recorded by national surveys. By assisting the poor and severely food insecure Palestinian households in Gaza and Bedouin and herding communities in West Bank’s Area C, and by disseminating information on food and nutrition practices, WFP addresses the basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians and tackles one of the or root causes of some of the food insecurity levels recorded by the government institutions.
These interventions aim at improving the overall food security levels including nutrition and health status of the vulnerable Palestinians and therefore at increasing their coping abilities to sudden shocks in the market for access to food. 
The project also contributes to the Food Security Sector’s three objectives as well as to the National Policy Agenda 2017-2022 (policies on escaping poverty and strengthening social protection as well as meeting the basic needs of the communities) to ensure that the vulnerable Palestinians households basic food needs are met, by assisting households in enhancing their food security levels and by strengthening national institutions in implementing food security strategies and social security safety net programs to best identify and target food insecure and vulnerable Palestinians.

The specific activities will largely include cash based interventions that will target emergency crisis affected households of above IPC 3 level. The planned cash transfers which will include both conditional and unconditional transfers aimed to increase households’ purchasing power and improve access to food and basic need based on the calculated Minimum Expenditure Basket for Nugal (USD 116 according to the latest FSNAU urban mainin markets for September 2020). In addition the response will undertake livelihood protection activities consisting of seasonal farming input, livestock support and diversification of livelihood source to enhance the recovery initiatives of drop out pastoralist, farming and fishing households just emerging from the droughts, COVID-19 pandemic livelihood related disruptions and also cyclones that have hit the Coastal Districts of Nugal Region. The design of the structures and outputs of the project will be required to conform to the required to conform to SPHERE standards including the construction. The project will utilize the Somalia Cash Working Group (CWG) recommended work norms to ensure labour output and compensation based on individual labor input. Women and the disabled shall be prioritized and given suitable jobs within the rehabilitation works. The project is also designed to main stream protection principles and to promote access, safety and dignity for all beneficiaries and in particular women and girls from IDP camps and others who have faced increased risk of SGBV since the outbreak of COVID-19 pandemic. --- SOCIAL PROTECTION  Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic In support of the ERL Sector (Strengthened Communities and Participation), UNICEF, through this project in 2023, will further support its Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth (10-24 years), female and male and those with disabilities, to access social, civic and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration and at scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability and meaningful engagement through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support young women and men to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. 
UNICEF will promote the active and meaningful participation of young people brought together from different ages, genders, abilities and cultural and educational backgrounds to be agents of positive change in their communities. UNICEF will work in the following three pillars and related interventions: (1) Provide access to services and skills-building for adolescents and youth for enhanced employability. (2) Strengthen social, civic and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (3) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own project projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners including services providers, youth workers and young volunteers to improve the quality of provided services and enhance the evidence generation. UNICEF will support the scalable and sustainable approaches with national partners including integrated centers & platforms.
In this project, UNICEF will give priority to adolescents and youth in the high severity areas such as Dara’a, Rural Damascus, Northern Homs, Southern Hama, East and Northeast of Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb. UNICEF will expand its support to young people in NES, focusing on returnees and displaced people in Raqqa and Hasakah, including those in camps, collective shelters and urban settings. UNICEF will focus on the most deprived areas in rural and urban areas. These will include camps (Hol, Roj, Newroz, Areesha, Mahmoudli) in Al-Hasakeh and Raqqa , the collective shelters in Al-Hasakeh city, and the rural areas in Qamishli, Malikia, Yaroubia, and Raqqa Governorate. Projects engaging young people will be essential needs for their effective integration in their communities. In addition, since 2014, many young people have been staying in camps and collective shelters. They do not enjoy the freedom of movement and face other risks, thus offering them activities that will enhance their skills and allow them to catch up to their peers in terms of skills and non-formal education.  The programme will coordinate with and support other UNICEF programmes to ensure interventions are tailored to the particular needs of young people. SHO funds for Social Protection  Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic Needs: Young people in Syria face a myriad of interrelated barriers that prevent their meaningful economic, social, and civic participation and engagement. They face stigma and discrimination regarding their capacities to lead positive change in their communities. Limited opportunities for economic, social, and civic engagement, particularly for the most marginalized adolescents and youth, contribute to their systematic exclusion and exacerbate feelings of isolation and disenfranchisement. However, experiences from other contexts of protracted crisis have shown that supporting young people’s social and civic engagement can have positive social outcomes and be conducive to increased community resilience and social cohesion.
Intervention: In support of the ERL Sector, UNICEF will further its support for the Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth, both female and male, as well as those with disabilities, to access social, civic, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration, and at-scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability, and meaningful engagement through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support 342,883 young women and men per year to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement, and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. UNICEF will work in the following two pillars and related interventions: (1) Strengthen social, civic, and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (2) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners, including services providers, youth workers, and young volunteers, to improve the quality of provided services and enhance evidence generation.
Protection Risk Analysis: After enduring 12 years of conflict and ongoing economic turmoil, young Syrians have faced devastating hardships that have eroded their resilience. This has particularly affected girls, who have resorted to harmful coping mechanisms such as dropping out of school, engaging in addictive behaviors, entering child labor, and marrying early. Social norms in many communities also hinder girls' and people with disabilities' participation in sports, cultural activities, and community engagement. The compounding effects of COVID-19, earthquakes, and economic challenges have exacerbated these risks. UNICEF will continue to mainstream the principles of safety, dignity, and do no harm, as well as the inclusive and meaningful access of the most marginalized boys and girls, especially those who live with disabilities, to ensure that no one is left behind. UNICEF will increase safe access to skills development, social cohesion, awareness-raising, and engagement opportunities. UNICEF will prioritize developing the capacity of the implementing partners through providing technical support in the fields of Child Safeguarding, Code of Conduct, and PSEA.
Risks: Economic deterioration and transportation barriers, along with potential conflicts between IDPs and host communities, as well as risks of exploitation or abuse. To address these risks, there will be capacity building for staff and volunteers, awareness campaigns on risks, mandatory screening during recruitment, establishing complaint mechanisms with adequate staff for follow-up, and ensuring data protection and confidentiality.

Assumptions: The project assumes support for integrated and joint approaches and the promotion of youth participation nationwide.

--- SOCIAL PROTECTION Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic In support of the ERL Sector (Strengthened Communities and Participation), UNICEF, through this project in 2023, will further support its Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth (10-24 years), female and male and those with disabilities, to access social, civic and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration and at scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability and meaningful engagement through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support young women and men to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. 
UNICEF will promote the active and meaningful participation of young people brought together from different ages, genders, abilities and cultural and educational backgrounds to be agents of positive change in their communities. UNICEF will work in the following three pillars and related interventions: (1) Provide access to services and skills-building for adolescents and youth for enhanced employability. (2) Strengthen social, civic and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (3) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own project projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners including services providers, youth workers and young volunteers to improve the quality of provided services and enhance the evidence generation. UNICEF will support the scalable and sustainable approaches with national partners including integrated centers & platforms.
In this project, UNICEF will give priority to adolescents and youth in the high severity areas such as Dara’a, Rural Damascus, Northern Homs, Southern Hama, East and Northeast of Aleppo, Deir-ez-Zor and Idleb. UNICEF will expand its support to young people in NES, focusing on returnees and displaced people in Raqqa and Hasakah, including those in camps, collective shelters and urban settings. UNICEF will focus on the most deprived areas in rural and urban areas. These will include camps (Hol, Roj, Newroz, Areesha, Mahmoudli) in Al-Hasakeh and Raqqa , the collective shelters in Al-Hasakeh city, and the rural areas in Qamishli, Malikia, Yaroubia, and Raqqa Governorate. Projects engaging young people will be essential needs for their effective integration in their communities. In addition, since 2014, many young people have been staying in camps and collective shelters. They do not enjoy the freedom of movement and face other risks, thus offering them activities that will enhance their skills and allow them to catch up to their peers in terms of skills and non-formal education.  The programme will coordinate with and support other UNICEF programmes to ensure interventions are tailored to the particular needs of young people. The programme will implement activities for young people affected by, or at high risk of, emergencies or the socio-economic situation, to acquire the right skills, become empowered and resilient community members who help their communities to cope with emergencies. Life-skills and citizenship education for these adolescents will equip and empower them to act as both participants and catalysts of change in their community as volunteers and peer influencers.

Improved immediate access to livelihoods for food insecure vulnerable households in drought affected populations and IDPs in Garowe district -Puntland state of Somalia Provision of Immediate food assistance to crisis and locust affected vulnerable IDPs and Host Community in Garowe, Eyl,  Dangorayo and Godobjiraan Districts. The response will cover Nugaal Region and target 28,500 beneficiaries (13,965 male and 14,535 female). The project will target mainly internally displaced households, refugee returnees and very poor host community households severely affected by droughts and conflicts across the populations groups of IDPS, Rural Pastoralist, Agro-pastoralist and fishing in the 4 target Districts of Garowe, Eyl, Dangorayo and Godobjiraan. The specific activities will largely include cash based interventions that will target emergency crisis affected households of above IPC 3 level. The planned cash transfers which will include both conditional and unconditional transfers aimed to increase households’ purchasing power and improve access to food and basic need based on the calculated Minimum Expenditure Basket for Nugal (USD 116 according to the latest FSNAU urban mainin markets for September 2020). In addition the response will undertake livelihood protection activities consisting of seasonal farming input, livestock support and diversification of livelihood source to enhance the recovery initiatives of drop out pastoralist, farming and fishing households just emerging from the droughts, COVID-19 pandemic livelihood related disruptions and also cyclones that have hit the Coastal Districts of Nugal Region. The design of the structures and outputs of the project will be required to conform to the required to conform to SPHERE standards including the construction. The project will utilize the Somalia Cash Working Group (CWG) recommended work norms to ensure labour output and compensation based on individual labor input. Women and the disabled shall be prioritized and given suitable jobs within the rehabilitation works. The project is also designed to main stream protection principles and to promote access, safety and dignity for all beneficiaries and in particular women and girls from IDP camps and others who have faced increased risk of SGBV since the outbreak of COVID-19 pandemic. The project is also designed to main stream protection principles and to promote access, safety and dignity for all beneficiaries and in particular women and girls from IDP camps and others who have faced increased risk of SGBV since the outbreak of COVID-19 pandemic. This will include promoting safety and dignity and avoiding to cause harm and ensure impartial and neutral services delivery all the targeted beneficiaries based purely on needs as per the protection requirements for livelihood programming. The project will equally ensure gender mainstreaming approaches remains key to its implementation. Wide consultation will also be made with the community leadership to develop an all accepted selection based on Community Based Targeting (CBT) selection criteria that will prioritize the most vulnerable households as beneficiaries prioritizing women and children access to the support. These will include women headed households, households with elderly and disable individual and large size poor families and IDP households, rural and fishing households with none or minimal sources of income. Provision of Seasonal inputs: The project will provide seasonal inputs consisting of farming seeds, harvest storage bags to cut on post-harvesting losses, fishing inputs for the fishery livelihood group in Eyr District and veterinary and feeds support to pastoralists in the 4 target Districts. The project will put in place a feedback mechanism to help get the beneficiaries share information related to the project. This will be an important component of the project as it will help guide the implementation process, capturing important details relating to changing needs by beneficiaries especially in view of the locusts and drought situation which has the potential to worsen.  The feedback mechanism shall also to collect complaints expressed by the beneficiaries for action by the project management.  In future the beneficiary data should be encrypted.

Country Strategic Plan for food assistance to the poor and severely food insecure population in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip WFP is committed to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and is guided by a strategic, programmatic and governance instrument to operationalize its plan and achieve its project objectives to: 
• End Hunger by protecting access to food and by improving dietary diversity;
• Support the implementation of the SDGs by enhancing the capacities of national institutions to implement food security strategies and operations;
This project directly contributes to strategic objectives two and three of the Humanitarian Response Plan 2018 2020, by meeting the basic food needs of severely vulnerable Palestinians and by improving their dietary diversity. 
WFP’s interventions focus on high food insecurity levels, including the malnutrition levels recorded by national surveys. By assisting the poor and severely food insecure Palestinian households in Gaza and Bedouin and herding communities in West Bank’s Area C, and by disseminating information on food and nutrition practices, WFP addresses the basic needs of vulnerable Palestinians and tackles one of the or root causes of some of the food insecurity levels recorded by the government institutions.
These interventions aim at improving the overall food security levels including nutrition and health status of the vulnerable Palestinians and therefore at increasing their coping abilities to sudden shocks in the market for access to food. 
The project also contributes to the Food Security Sector’s three objectives as well as to the National Policy Agenda 2017-2022 (policies on escaping poverty and strengthening social protection as well as meeting the basic needs of the communities) to ensure that the vulnerable Palestinians households basic food needs are met, by assisting households in enhancing their food security levels and by strengthening national institutions in implementing food security strategies and social security safety net programs to best identify and target food insecure and vulnerable Palestinians.

SHO funds for Social Protection Expanding Social, Civic and Economic Engagement and Social Cohesion Interventions for Conﬂict-Affected Adolescents and Youth in the Syrian Arab Republic Needs: Young people in Syria face a myriad of interrelated barriers that prevent their meaningful economic, social, and civic participation and engagement. They face stigma and discrimination regarding their capacities to lead positive change in their communities. Limited opportunities for economic, social, and civic engagement, particularly for the most marginalized adolescents and youth, contribute to their systematic exclusion and exacerbate feelings of isolation and disenfranchisement. However, experiences from other contexts of protracted crisis have shown that supporting young people’s social and civic engagement can have positive social outcomes and be conducive to increased community resilience and social cohesion.
Intervention: In support of the ERL Sector, UNICEF will further its support for the Generation Unlimited initiative and No Lost Generation Agenda by empowering vulnerable adolescents and youth, both female and male, as well as those with disabilities, to access social, civic, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement (including participation in social cohesion initiatives) with the objective of contributing to enhancing resilience and social cohesion. UNICEF will build on strategic partnerships, integration, and at-scale programming focusing on the most vulnerable adolescents to strengthen skills development, employability, and meaningful engagement through friendly spaces and mobile teams. The proposed project will support 342,883 young women and men per year to have better access to civic, social, and economic opportunities for skill development and engagement, and to unleash their potentials and increase their learning, leadership, and employability opportunities. UNICEF will work in the following two pillars and related interventions: (1) Strengthen social, civic, and economic engagement of adolescents and youth and foster volunteerism and social cohesion-building. (2) Support young entrepreneurs to start their own projects through seed funding. UNICEF will continue strengthening the capacity of local partners, including services providers, youth workers, and young volunteers, to improve the quality of provided services and enhance evidence generation.
Protection Risk Analysis: After enduring 12 years of conflict and ongoing economic turmoil, young Syrians have faced devastating hardships that have eroded their resilience. This has particularly affected girls, who have resorted to harmful coping mechanisms such as dropping out of school, engaging in addictive behaviors, entering child labor, and marrying early. Social norms in many communities also hinder girls' and people with disabilities' participation in sports, cultural activities, and community engagement. The compounding effects of COVID-19, earthquakes, and economic challenges have exacerbated these risks. UNICEF will continue to mainstream the principles of safety, dignity, and do no harm, as well as the inclusive and meaningful access of the most marginalized boys and girls, especially those who live with disabilities, to ensure that no one is left behind. UNICEF will increase safe access to skills development, social cohesion, awareness-raising, and engagement opportunities. UNICEF will prioritize developing the capacity of the implementing partners through providing technical support in the fields of Child Safeguarding, Code of Conduct, and PSEA.
Risks: Economic deterioration and transportation barriers, along with potential conflicts between IDPs and host communities, as well as risks of exploitation or abuse. To address these risks, there will be capacity building for staff and volunteers, awareness campaigns on risks, mandatory screening during recruitment, establishing complaint mechanisms with adequate staff for follow-up, and ensuring data protection and confidentiality.

Assumptions: The project assumes support for integrated and joint approaches and the promotion of youth participation nationwide.

Against Nigeria HRP Improvement of the Protection of People of Concern in North East Nigeria Through the Provision of Shelter and NFI Assistance. This project will target IDPs and returnees in three affected states, Yobe, Adamawa and Borno with provision of emergency shelters, Non-food Items (NFIs), transitional and shelter repair kits as protection live-saving assistance aligned with Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM Sector strategic objectives for the HRP 2019. In 2019 UNHCR continued to effectively respond to shelter needs and aims to target a total of 69,569 households, 347,846 individuals in formal and informal camps and newly accessible areas by the end of the year. As the number of returns and displacement increases due to military operations, there is need to provide shelter related assistance for returnees who are residing in their plots and as well as for host families whose resources have been overstretched. Subsequently acknowledging that the humanitarian situation is still unpredictable; there is need to provide shelters and NFIs for life-saving emergency assistance to promote the protection, safety and dignity of affected Persons of Concern (PoCs). Despite the achievements in the past, the continuous needs for IDPs, though shaped by very different dynamics, revealed that quite a significant majority of people are living in congested camps. The needs assessment conducted in 2019 by Shelter/ NFI/ CCCM sector indicated that as of end of June 2019, 3809 IDP households were living without shelter and NFI assistance since their arrival. In addition to that, 7593 households living in partitioned communal shelters needed NFIs and dignified emergency shelters. The ongoing and protracted displacement leaves the affected people in need of other humanitarian assistance such as Food, WASH, and Health among others. In 2020, UNHCR shall build upon progress being made in 2019 and proposes to respond to unmet needs in Adamawa (Mubi North, Mubi South, Madagali, Michika, Yola South and Yola north); Borno (Bama, Banki, Damasak, Damboa, Dikwa, Jere, konduga, Gwoza, Pulka, Maiduguri, Mobbar, Monguno, Rann and Ngala) and Yobe State (Damaturu and Gujba,) through provision of; - (1) 7,000 Emergency shelters (2) 52,129 NFIs kits to IDPs in both formal and informal camps (3) 10,440 Shelter repair kits to returnees with the provision of conditional CASH component of NGN 30,000 Naira adequate to cover for the cost labor and molding of mud bricks among other unforeseen needs. All the shelters are designed to cater for Women, Men, Girls and boys, persons with specific needs and partitioned to mitigate SGBV cases. The selection of beneficiaries will be based on needs assessment and vulnerability screening in the locations at the time of implementation. Identification and verification of beneficiaries are guided by UNHCR’s Protection principles, and endorsed by community leaders, NEMA, and SEMA officials at LGA areas. UNHCR will reinforce a transparent process of beneficiary selection and the prioritization of needs of vulnerable groups. The project targets the IDPs and Returnees households suffering from protracted displacement and returning home. UNHCR will work to ensure that potential beneficiaries are aware of their responsibilities during the project and of options available to them. It is important to recognize that not everyone can manage the construction/ repair of their own house and that their time might be better used to generate income. The families’ decision to participate in this programme will be achieved through sensitization meetings, detailed assessments, participatory planning and prioritizing the provision of technical training and capacity building. A community-based feedback mechanism through regular mass meetings and focus group discussions will be established to enable IDPs express their opinions on issues affecting their assistance need. The discussions will also provide beneficiaries the opportunity to understand the shelter selection and allocation process.

While the overall Global acute malnutrition (GAM) remains at 13.6%, the prevalence of GAM varies significantly across the localities with very high situation (GAM above 15% and above as per WHO classification) reported in 64 localities. The proposed nutrition project aim is to improve equitable access to quality life-saving curative and preventive services through the systematic provision of nutrition services in South Kordofan, North Kordofan, Central Darfur, North Darfur, West Darfur, Sennar, Blue Nile and Red Sea states in which 29 localities will be covered. Vulnerable children under-five and PLWs are the main target of the project. Through SC -Nutrition interventions, a total of 362,874 beneficiaries will benefit from the services provided, among them (87,131 boys, 90,680 girls, 184,383 women, 680 men). Save the children will implement lifesaving, preventative interventions, treatment of severe and moderate acute malnutrition among children under five years and Pregnant and Lactating Women (PLWs), referral of SAM children with medical complications and minor rehabilitation to nutrition sites. To reach the estimated targets and planned response scale up, the nutrition sector will deploy integrated response modalities with health sector, WASH, FSL, protection, education at facility and community levels. SC will deliver nutrition services through existing health facilities, mobile and outreach teams and at community such as mother-to mother support groups activities including IDPs and hard to reach areas, use of cash-based interventions to increase access and utilization of nutrition services through FSL will be used for most cases in need. Immediate Food Assistance for Internally Displaced Persons(IDPs) in the Far North (40,000 Beneficiaries) Immediate Food Assistance for Internally Displaced Persons(IDPs) in the Far North (40,000 Beneficiaries)  In the Far North region, the Boko Haram insurgency in Nigeria has displaced 100,504 Nigerian refugees in Cameroon as of October 2018, and 98,590 of them live in the Far North region (UNHCR, October 2018). Boko Haram attacks have also resulted in 227,581 internally displaced persons (IDPs) (UNHCR, October 2018), who are struggling to survive in strenuous conditions in villages or small towns in the area. The region is predominantly arid and regularly hit by drought and seasonal floods. Access to basic services is also more limited than in other regions of the country. The arrival of IDPs in food-insecure areas has severely affected host communities as well. This has put enormous pressure on already scarce community resources and the local economy by reducing farm productivity and access to land and food markets. Boko Haram attacks have disrupted the economic, agricultural, and pastoral activities in the Far North region, causing a depletion of livelihoods and household assets. As a consequence, the existing chronic vulnerability and structural food insecurity have been aggravated. IDPs have fleed from the bordering regions where the Boko Haram attacks have occurred but the vulnerable IDP households live without means or assets to support themselves. To address the urgent food needs of the most vulnerable IDPs, WFP plans to provide immediate food assistance with full ration to the most vulnerable 40,000 IDPs in the Far North for 12 months in 2019. 25,000 beneficiaries will be supported with the in-kind food assistance and the rest 15,000 with Cash-Based Transfer(CBT).

Improved access to water for drought-affected communities in Las Anod Emergency WASH Response for people affected by emergency in Somaliland/Somalia  The humanitarian situation in Somalia remains critical due to the ongoing impacts of drought, conflict, locust infestation, and the COVID 19 pandemic. An estimated 6.61 million people, about 42 per cent of the Somali population are in need of emergency life-saving WASH assistance of which 4.2 million will need safe drinking water, 3.2 million sanitation services, and 5.2 million hygiene supplies. According to FAO/SWALIM draught analysis from 2000 to July 2021, the trend shows that Somalia has been experiencing cyclic drought every five to six years: 2000/2001, 2004/2005, 2010/2011, 2016/2017, and currently in 2020/2021. These drought conditions were triggered by consecutive seasons of below-average rainfall including the below-average Gu rains (April to July 2021) and delay of short Dayr rains (October to December 2021). The Somalia Food Security Cluster as of 18th October 2021 confirms that half of Somalia is still experiencing serious drought conditions (moderate to severe drought with water shortages and livestock losses), with the worst impacts being felt in Jubaland, South West State, Galmudug, and areas of Puntland. The Deyr seasonal rainfall is expected to be below average, with depressed rains not going to be effective in mitigating drought conditions. A devastating drought is likely to continue into 2022 given the 1) La Nina conditions, 2) poor rainfall forecast for October and November and 3) existing drought conditions.
Access to water is mainly dependent on rainfall in the majority of the country. Barkads in nonriverine areas are the major water sources while others depend on shallow/deep groundwater sources. Thus, failure in rains triggers massive shortages as currently being reported from Jubaland, Part of Somaliland, Galmudug, and many other areas. 50 of the 74 districts in Somalia faced severe water shortages and water prices increased by 66 per cent7 in Gedo, Galgadud, Mudug, Sool, and Sanaag regions (JMCNA 2021). The Non-functionality of few strategic boreholes also increases as the operation hours increase. Many shallow-water sources are drying while others are having increased brackish water intrusions. Over 39% of Somalis don’t have access to sustained, improved and safe water. As result, over 84% are walking more than 15minuts to access water while over 92% don’t have water collection and storage facilities. Due to limited access and poor quality of existing water sources, over 1.3 million people in 24 drought-affected locations are dependent on water trucking – the majority of them are private water trucking. Oxfam PDMs and HNO results confirm the majority of Somalis use two jerry cans per day during drought conditions. 39% of people assessed confirm they wash their hands but have reported having no access to soap. 45% of girls assessed have reported having access to Menstruation hygiene management (MHM) materials at or can access from local markets.
Oxfam has been working in Somalia for over 40 years and will continue to provide life-saving humanitarian support and build the capacity of both private and public institutions. Oxfam is working with over 10 national NGOs in a different part of Somalia. In response to the continued emergency, Oxfam will continue supporting efforts to nation/local government in containment and prevention of COVID-19, will monitor and rehabilitate non-function strategic boreholes, will conduct expansion of existing water sources in order to reduce the walking time, will drill boreholes in chronically water insecure areas, will provide cash and voucher assistant for people to access live-saving water, hygiene and MHM kits from local markets or access point established by Oxfam, will work with community health volunteers to increase awareness and handwashing practice during critical times and will construct shared household latrines for communities practicing open defecations.

Improved Immediate Access to Food for Vulnerable IDPs in Dayniile District, Mogadishu in Banadir Region Support for Life Saving and Restoration of livelihoods for Vulnerable Populations in Benadir, Lower Shabelle and Galmudug Regions. Somalia continues to face a dire humanitarian situation, with an estimated 5.2 million people in need of humanitarian assistance. This is attributed to cumulative shocks, including erratic 2020 Gu season, widespread and severe seasonal flooding, desert locust infestation, socio-economic impacts of COVID-19 and protracted conflict and flood-related displacements.

According to the 2020 Post Gu Seasonal Food Security and Nutrition Analysis for September (FAO/FSNAU), an estimated 1.3 million people are facing Crisis or worse (IPC Phase 3 or higher) outcomes through September 2020. This number is expected to increase to 2.1 million people through December 2020, in the absence of humanitarian assistance. An additional 2.5 million people are Stressed (IPC Phase 2), bringing the total number of people experiencing acute food insecurity to 3.8 million. In addition, 849,900 children under the age of five years face acute malnutrition over the next 12 months (September 2020 to August 2021), including 143,400 likely to be severely malnourished.

The ongoing Deyr rains in parts of central regions of Galmudug pose a high risk of flash flooding especially in low-lying areas. In Baxda village, Caddado district, Mudug region, one person died following heavy rains that collapsed their house. According to a multi-agency assessment in Adado district in May 2020, about 1,350 IDP households and 350 households from vulnerable host community need food security intervention. Seasonal Hagaa flooding since July has resulted in the displacement of nearly 342,000 people, inundated 294 villages and destroyed property and about 15,000 to 20,000 hectares of assorted crops, mainly in rural areas along the Shabelle river valley according to the UNHCR-led Protection and Return Monitoring Network (PRMN) in Somalia. 

Desert locusts continue to cause havoc in different parts of Somalia. In Galmudug, adult locusts continue to spread in rural villages in Galkacyo, Hobyo, Cabudwaaq, Cadaado, and Dhuusamarreeb. The locust problem has a wide range of impacts that worry Galmudug pastoralist as the region’s economic mainstay is livestock rearing. The locust will have a long-term impact on grazing lands and the poor performance of the rainy seasons may lead to depletion of pasture and acceleration of the dry season. 

CPD plans to reach 23,400 people facing severe acute food insecurity in Galmudug, Benadir and Lower Shabelle regions, mainly IDPs and host communities affected by the impacts of floods, desert locusts, conflicts and socio-economic impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic by improving access to food through unconditional and conditional transfers. Weak, vulnerable members of the IDPs and the host communities such as women and child-headed households, people with disability and the elderly will receive unconditional support through mobile cash transfers as per the CWG recommended transfer values per region (Benadir $70, Galgadud $110, Lower Shabelle $60, Mudug $80).  The men and the youth will be engaged in conditional transfers e.g. cash/food-for-work for livelihood interventions that will support community recover their livelihood and meet their immediate needs. Activities include rehabilitation and establishment of community infrastructure such as water catchments i.e. water pans.

CPD will protect and restore livelihoods related to food and income sources for the target communities through skills training to increase household income; rehabilitation and support for productive capacities of communities through agricultural inputs (e.g. quality seed, farm tools, training, land preparation and irrigation support) and livelihood strengthening and diversification (e.g. fishing).

Project will be inclusive by incorporating people with disability, women, youth and marginalized groups in all project phases in the target areas. Covid-19 measures and guidelines will be incorporated in project implementation.

Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) in oPt - Phase I Informing the humanitarian response in the occupied Palestinian territories through multi-sector, evidence-based monitoring, assessments, and analysis Through this proposed action, REACH (a joint initiative of ACTED, IMPACT Initiatives and UNOSAT) will support the coordination and technical implementation of two initiatives: a Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) and a Joint Market Monitoring initiative, to provide evidence on vulnerabilities and market dynamics throughout the West Bank and Gaza. 

The MSNA will consist of a multi-sectoral household survey employed among a representative sample of the affected population in both the West Bank and Gaza. The MSNA will be conducted in partnership with OCHA oPt and within the framework of the wider development and humanitarian architecture. As in 2021, household data for the MSNA will be collected in partnership with the Palestinian Central Bureau for Statistics (PCBS). Central to this collaborative data partnership are strategies and protection measures, including specific channels to ensure accountability to affected populations, the most vital of which is a dedicated strategy and platform to ensure complaint mechanisms are accessible, properly communicated, and relevant to all population groups according to CBCM SOPs.

The proposed MSNA and JMMI will aim to achieve the following objectives:

1. Directly inform joint humanitarian-development response planning based on the nexus approach that the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) has adopted beginning in 2022, through the provision of comprehensive, multi-sectoral household data as well as monitoring and reporting of market prices and availability dynamics. Data from both the MSNA and JMMI will therefore aim to inform the development of both the 2023 HNO/HRP and further support the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework planned for 2023-27;

2. Provide a detailed inter-sectoral analysis of the magnitude and severity of humanitarian needs among crisis-affected populations in oPt, to support the calculation of sectoral and overall People in Need (PiN) and severity calculations.

3. Provide a detailed vulnerability analysis to identify at-risk and ‘furthest left behind’ population groups, as well as geographic areas with the most acute needs and vulnerabilities, to subsequently inform assistance targeting and response planning efforts; 

4. Support inclusive and people-centred assistance provision based on the principles of Accountability to Affected Populations (AAP), through the collection of information regarding preferred communication, information sharing, and assistance modalities. 

5. To improve access to timely and accurate regional and nationwide data through the harmonized joint market monitoring framework that will provide evolutions in prices, market functionality/access, and household expenditure to inform cash transfer programming, development programmes and identify contextual factors (both historically and on a monthly basis) that might affect market dynamics to support cash-based interventions for programmatic actors.  

REACH will produce the following key outputs: 
1 clean, anonymized multi-sectoral needs household dataset; 
1 static summary findings dashboard; series of presentations to key stakeholders; 
1 package of six sectoral factsheets; 
1 final analytical report (MSNA Bulletin)
1 Interactive/dynamic Market Monitoring dashboard
2 Static infographics on Survival Minimum Expenditure Basket (SMEB)/Cash Transfer Value (CTV) and price indexes
2 Static infographics on market functionality and goods availability.
1 final JMMI report/findings summary

Multi-sectoral project for community resilience Comprehensive humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations affected by the military conflict in eastern Ukraine and / or COVID-19 with a focus on access to food and income opportunities The FSL project aims to improve the food security for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men in conflict-affected areas and put at greater risks in the face of COVID-19, and support women and men engage in sustainable livelihoods, in the agriculture and in other sectors alike. Through enhanced targeting of particularly underserved communities and enhanced community-based approach, the project covers three levels of actions, from immediate relief, through self-sufficiency, and longer-term resilience. It will invest special attention and efforts to support both transition in GCA and responding to enduring humanitarian needs in NGCA, and integrate the age, gender and diversity factors influencing food security and livelihoods, including factors of feminised poverty and care dependency.
At a first level the project aims to ‘ensure immediate access to food’ for the most vulnerable women, girls, boys and men living along the ‘line of contact’ in both Luhansk and Donetsk NGCA. The assistance will take the form of food vouchers, and be organised through quarterly rounds to take account of seasonal variations. In addition, PIN will provide short-term, immediate assistance in the form of food kits for those most at risk in the face of COVID-19. Through this modality, those individuals with greater health risks and no direct support system will have access to food items while minimising their exposure to COVID-19 infection risks.
At a second level, in GCA the project will then aim to improve longer-term, sustainable food security for women and men and their households with access to small landplots near the LoC. Such assistance will take the form of seasonal activities, with distribution of vouchers for seeds, of drip irrigation kits, and delivery of trainings. It will enable smallholder farmers in underserved communities to increase their self-sufficiency throughout the year. As such the project will directly contribute to the cluster objective to ‘Improve food security through the provision of emergency and time-critical agriculture assistance’.
At a third level, in GCA the project will eventually aim to support access to employment and micro-, small businesses for women and men in communities near the LoC. Trainings will be held, not only on employment, vocational and business-related topics, but also to foster individual empowerment. Special attention will be paid to support women- and youth-led entreprises for equal access to opportunities and as vectors of development for their entire communities. On short-term and seasonable basis, cash-for-work opportunities will be created around community needs, whether to rehabilitate priority infrastructure or realise other community-based initiatives, account taken of age, gender and diversity. This will serve both poverty reduction, community social cohesion and living conditions in the communities. As such the project will directly contribute to the cluster objective to ‘Enhance resilience of vulnerable people affected by conflict and/or COVID-19 through restoring of non-agriculture livelihood and promote resilience to shocks (including wildfire, unemployment, higher prices, and other hazard) at community level’. 
Throughout these actions, PIN will maintain a robust Community Feedback and Accountability Mechanism though its community-based approach and engagement with women, girls, boys, men, elderly and people with disabilities to raise their voices; enhanced consultations and testing of participation and social accountability mechanisms; feedback and complaints hotline, response, referrals and analysis for further adjustment of the assistance.

Multi-sectoral Response in Kassala State Access to Humanitarian life-saving child protection and GBV response services in North Darfur, North / South Kordofan and White Nile states The project objective is to protect people from violence, neglect, and exploitation by providing access to life-saving child protection and GBV response services to targeted communities in White Nile, North Kordofan, and North Darfur. In order to accomplish this, Plan will provide high quality protection services and contribute to community stabilization and resilience. Protection services and capacity building activities will include: CP and GBV case management, distribution of dignity kits to vulnerable girls, multi-purpose cash transfer to vulnerable households and hosting UASC, and referrals mechanisms including to Family and Child Protection Units, training of social workers and partner staff on GBV, CP, and referral pathways, and psychosocial support to conflict affected children and youth. The provision of protection services must be paired with activities to increase knowledge of and access to those services. Therefore, Plan will also establish/strengthen and equip Community Based Child Protection Networks (CBCPNs), conduct community awareness session of CP, FGM, SEA and child marriage risks, and conduct sensitization on GBV prevention and response. Plan will foster communal stability and resilience by providing life skills training, parenting sessions, conducting community awareness sessions on peacebuilding and conflict transformation, and training duty bearers and community leaders on peacebuilding.  Additionally, Plan will establish child-friendly community feedback and response mechanisms so that all project beneficiaries are able to provide feedback and file complaints.

SC will deliver nutrition services through existing health facilities, mobile and outreach teams and at community such as mother-to mother support groups activities including IDPs and hard to reach areas, use of cash-based interventions to increase access and utilization of nutrition services through FSL will be used for most cases in need. The nutrition response will also target the total under-five and PLW with preventive nutrition services e.g. micronutrient supplementation to ensure levels of acute malnutrition are not above average thresholds, and to also reduce morbidity and mortality. The response will prioritise households with persons living with disabilities, who face barriers in accessing health, nutrition and WASH services and are disproportionately food insecure due to high levels of exclusion. 
The nutrition status of the targeted population in the BAY states significantly deteriorates during the period from May-August every year, which is the lean season and coincides with the rainy season. The season is characterised by very high rates of acute malnutrition with medical complications due to poor food access and a high prevalence of diarrhoea and malaria. UNICEF will need to adequately prepare for the lean season period by prepositioning supplies, increasing the overall sector capacity to treat acute malnutrition with a focus on inpatient care and IYCF-E
The nutrition response in BAY states will be contextualised in 2022 based on the following categorisation: 
1. Protracted crisis e.g north and central Borno LGAs where the rates of acute malnutrition are high, worsened by poor access to food and health systems. The approach in these areas will include INGO/NNGO direct support to the affected population, and prioritisation of lifesaving nutrition activities. 
3. New emergencies – locations of new crisis and fluctuations such as relocations, displacements and spike in acute malnutrition. The approach will focus on the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with a focus on lifesaving activities. 
4. Hard-to-reach / inaccessible areas – locations with limited humanitarian footprints and access e.g Gubio and Magumeri. The approach will include RRM and remote management strategy (where feasible) with a focus on life-saving interventions. UNICEF will also strengthen the implementation of nutrition interventions through local organizations or community-based structures to implement nutrition services in hard-to-reach/inaccessible areas. 
UNICEF response is primarily through services and in-kind deliveries. UNICEF will employ the use of cash and voucher assistance (CVA) to fill the nutrient gap in the Nutrition/Food Minimum Expenditure Basket to ensure that populations have access to a varied diet e.g CVA for meats and vegetables. 
The nutrition status of the affected population is an outcome of various underlying issues including access to health, WASH, food security, child protection, and gender issues. The main cause of acute malnutrition among children and women in BAY states is the high morbidity rates. High diarrhoea prevalence is the major cause of acute malnutrition among the IDPs and urban poor population due to the prevailing poor hygiene and sanitation conditions worsened by congested living conditions. The response will strengthen the integration of nutrition-sensitive interventions including WASH, food security, health, livelihoods and child protection, and gender-based violence risk mitigation.
UNICEF will prioritise projects that include basic nutrition packages such as integrated treatment of acute malnutrition (SAM and MAM) and prevention services including integration with WASH, food security, health and protections services.

There is a serious risk that the impact of consecutive below average to poor rainfall in most parts of the country will develop into a severe drought by early to mid- 2022 with the number of people facing acute food insecurity on the rise. It is likely that minority groups, women, children, people with disabilities, will experience heightened protection risks as a result, unless they are intentionally targeted to receive tailored assistance.

With approximately 3.5 million individuals in IPC 3 and 4 through at least December 2021, FAO proposes to target 160,300 households (961,800 individuals- 91,500 IDPs and 870,300 non- IDPs) in IPC 3 and IPC 4 caseloads respectively. This will include 216,790 women, 254,492 girls, 264,880 boys and 225,638 men and 144,270 people living with disabilities (PWD) across 59 districts in Somalia through its flagship Cash+ approach combining short-term cash transfers with tailored livelihood support in accordance with technical and humanitarian standards. Vulnerable households will identified from at-risk pastoral, agro-pastoral, fishing, riverine farmers, IDPs and Non- IDP communities in IPC 3 and 4 areas. This intervention will integrate short-term cash transfers aimed at enabling the most vulnerable households to meet their immediate needs, with livelihood support to allow crisis-affected households to get back into production. FAO will employ community- led beneficiary selection processes and ensure adequate targeting and representation of extremely vulnerable and minority groups in community committees. Interventions proposed will employ a Do No Harm approach with a gender lens that ensures conflict- sensitivity to reduce protection risks for all individuals, and to mitigate the risk of conflict or community tensions. 

Under Food Security Cluster (FSC) Objective 1, to improve access to food, FAO will deliver lifesaving cash assistance to 160,300 households through a blend of conditional (Cash-for-Work) and unconditional (UCT) transfers. Under UCT, FAO will prioritize Cash+ interventions including Cash+ Agriculture, Cash+ livestock and Cash+ fisheries. These modalities will increase households’ immediate access to food by providing sufficient cash to access the minimum expenditure basket (MEB), while supporting the rehabilitation of critical productive and community infrastructure. It will also boost household food production, increase household incomes and create employment opportunities. Cash transfer values will be informed by the Cash Working Group and are expected to differ per district/ region of intervention. They, however, will be valued at 80 percent of the food MEB, which can range from USD 50- 100 per month. All cash-based programmes will include training on good nutrition practices. 

Under FSC Objective 2, to protect livelihoods and related food sources, FAO will provide in-kind, technical support and tailored trainings to 112,500 HHs to anticipate, mitigate and respond to food security and nutrition threats, including the delivery of integrated cash and livelihood support to targeted HHs. In addition, FAO shall provide transitional cash support to 13,100 HHs across agro pastoral, pastoral and fishing livelihood zones to augment the adaptive capacity of HHs, strengthen and foster resilience to future shocks, cushioning them from food insecurity and malnutrition. Trainings shall be delivered alongside input provision to build skills in sustainable use of resources provided, build skills in livelihoods management including harvest, post- harvest management, linking beneficiaries to long- term interventions that provide them opportunities to enhance their livelihoods and skills.

Seguridad alimentaria - Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela Programa de seguridad alimentaria basado en la escuela  Con el objetivo de contribuir a la seguridad alimentaria de la población con mayores necesidades, el Programa Mundial de Alimentos de Naciones Unidas (WFP, por sus siglas en inglés) en Venezuela desarrolla un programa de asistencia humanitaria basado en la escuela para garantizar el acceso de los más vulnerables a una alimentación adecuada y nutritiva en el entorno escolar, familiar y comunitario. 
Este programa inició en 2021 con comidas escolares en emergencias priorizando escuelas iniciales y de educación especial.

WFP proporciona comidas escolares acompañado de un paquete integrado de intervenciones para mejorar el acceso a alimentos nutritivos y diversificados a través de las escuelas, contribuyendo al mismo tiempo a mejorar la salud y la nutrición de los niños en edad escolar, los estudiantes con discapacidad y el personal escolar, y apoyando a las comunidades a reducir la dependencia en estrategias de afrontamiento. De manera gradual, el WFP está realizando compras locales de alimentos, e incluyendo acciones para apoyar los mercados locales con compras a pequeños productores y apoyo técnico para acceso a mercados.

En este sentido, el programa de comidas escolares en emergencias tiene los siguientes componentes, para asegurar un enfoque integral que apoye al estudiante en el entorno escolar y familiar:

1. Entrega de comidas escolares nutritivas para estudiantes y personal escolar, promoviendo las compras locales y a pequeños productores.
2. Apoyo a la seguridad alimentaria del hogar.
3. Rehabilitación de cocinas escolares para garantizar condiciones adecuadas de preparación de alimentos.
4. Comunicación para sensibilizar acerca de los principios humanitarios, la adecuada preparación de alimentos, nutrición, higiene y mantenimiento de cocinas escolares.
5. Fortalecimiento de capacidades de socios implementadores y personal escolar.
6. Acciones sensibles a la nutrición, que incluyen, tamizaje en las escuelas, educación nutricional, referencia a servicios especializados y entrega de alimento complementario fortificado (Super Cereal Plus).

Support disaster affected populations in Hirshabelle, and Puntland states to protect their livelihoods and food security In June, Crisis (IPC 3) or Stressed (IPC 2) outcomes persist across the country. Nearly 20 percent of the total 2.7 million people in need of food assistance did not access it, including in riverine and rural areas of the South, where humanitarian access is low. The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the Somali economy is significant. Poor urban and IDP households, as well as pastoralists in northern Somalia, are likely to be most affected by an estimated 30-50 percent decline in annual external remittances, anticipated 25-35 percent decline in annual livestock exports, lower labor demand, and above-average imported staple food prices. In most IDP settlements and urban areas, at least 20 percent of the population still face food consumption gaps or are engaged in negative livelihoods coping strategies indicative of Crisis (IPC Phase 3) even after food assistance distributions. Additionally, Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes are expected from June to September in parts of central Somalia, where livestock holdings are lowest, and in northeastern Somalia, where the economy is more dependent on livestock, seafood, and frankincense exports. The erratic distribution of rainfall during the April to June gu season has worsened Gu cereal production prospects in south-central Somalia. During the July to September dry season, up to 3.5 million people are anticipated to be unable to meet their minimum food needs and in need of urgent humanitarian food assistance. Further, the NOAA/CPC NMME forecast predicts an increased likelihood of a below-average deyr rainfall season from October to December 2020. FEWS NET’S research shows the NMME forecast has a strong capability to predict below-average rainfall during the October to December rainfall season in eastern East Africa. Combined with the persistent threat of desert locust, the impact of below-average rains on crop and livestock production is expected to lead to widespread deterioration to Crisis (IPC Phase 3) in northern and central pastoral areas and southern agropastoral areas in the absence of sustained food assistance. The conflict between insurgents and the FGS – supported by AMISOM and other forces – and conflict between clans over the control of land and resource management is expected to continue to periodically restrict humanitarian access, cause loss of life and assets, cause displacement, and disrupt trade and population movements. Conflict is most likely to affect Bakool, Bay, Galgaduud, Gedo, Hiiraan, the Jubas, and the Shabelles regions. Thus, AADSOM will support disaster-affected populations in Hirshabelle, and Puntland to protect their livelihoods, support local food production, and prevent the adoption of crisis strategies. AADSOM will carry out the following activities to reach the above objectives:
1. AADSOM will increase access to food and improve nutrition through Unconditional Cash Transfer to crisis-affected and underserved 1,000 IDPs and host communities HHs in Bari, and Hiran regions, benefiting around 6,000 women, men, boys, and girls including disabled people and marginalized communities. The supporting period will be 3 months and the rate is 60% Minimum Expenditure Basket (MEB) which corresponding to 60 USD. 
2. Supporting 2000 farmers in Hiran and Bari regions with land preparation and input distribution; 
3. To keep the sustainability of the project and increase the production of the beneficiaries, AADSOM will train 100 selected lead farmers on Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) to increase their livelihoods production and adapt the new technologies. 
4. Rehabilitation of  5 primary canals in Hiran region through CFW, benefiting 500 workers for a period of three months, benefiting around 3,000 (450 men, 600 women, 900 girls, 900 boys and 150 disabilities). 
During the project implementation, women, men, children, disabled, marginalized communities, and IDPs will be heard their voices and consulted.

Raise awareness and hygiene kits for Covid 19 and a single cash transfer to HH Integrated COVID-19 WASH Response to the Rohingya  and Host population in Cox’s Bazar WaSH project is continuing to ensure inclusive and equitable provision of life saving water and sanitation services building on infrastructure already constructed in the previous phase in 2019 (in the Camp no,14 and 15 and host community) and strengthening behaviour change communication (BCC) by encouraging community-based collective measures. 
 There are two main routes of transmission of COVID-19: respiratory droplets and direct contact. Respiratory droplets are generated when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Droplets may also land on surfaces where the virus could remain viable and thus, the immediate environment of an infected individual can serve as a source of transmission (contact transmission). The provision of safe water, sanitation, hygienic living and environmental conditions are essential to protect human health during all infectious disease outbreaks, including the COVID-19outbreak. Hand hygiene, personal and social hygiene are key elements in preventing this disease to spread. As of today, a lot of aspects of COVID-19 prevention and control are still unclear, including implications related to WASH interventions (like virus persistence on surfaces or sewage). 

  The previous phase of the intervention has contributed to an increase in the appropriate usage of handwashing. Almost 79% of the respondents from the end of project evaluation reported that handwashing points installed under the project were utilized for hygiene maintenance. In terms of safe and inclusive access to water, the water point accessibility for PWD, pregnant women, adolescent girls and aged persons has been enhanced. The increase in ease of accessibility for pregnant women rose from 6% in baseline to 48%, similarly, for adolescent girls, it improved from 24% to 83%. So, maintenance of these essential WaSH facilities and services are vital to reduce the risk of disease outbreak.
Bear in mind the gravity of the issue, CAID will continue to ensure lifesaving water and sanitation services to the Rohingya and host communities in 2020. Focus will be provided to address the key challenges facing WaSH service such as congestion at water points, unequal distribution, inclusive access and protection concerns in bathing cubicles and latrines.

ARC understands that internal displacements are the key driver of humanitarian needs in Somalia. Many IDPs and Poor vulnerable Host communities are currently residing in Urban and pre-urban informal crowded areas with insufficient access to water and Sanitation. According to JMCNA assessment done in August by REACH, 53% of the IDPs face challenges in terms of access to WASH services in Somalia. The project is aimed at supporting the most vulnerable IDP families in Afgooye and Banadir to mitigate risks faced through Shelter/NFI interventions. It is expected that a total of 12,000 IDP(Elderly 600 men,1000 women, 4000 boys 1000 girls 3000, disabled 2,200 and non disabled 200) in Afgooye and Banadir will benefit from the distribution of emergency shelter kits and non-food items. Provision of NFI kits and ESKs will target the newly displaced persons and protracted IDPs with shelter structures that barely protect their dignity and privacy. The intervention is aimed at improving the living conditions of the IDPs by speeding up their recovery from damages caused by displacements.
2000 NFI kits and 2000 ESKs will be distributed through voucher and in kind respectively to 2000 IDP households. The in kind modality is influenced by SSWC's past experience with CBI where beneficiaries did not construct ESKs and channeled the money to other purposes. A market assessment will be conducted prior to the purchase of the items to ascertain their market prices. The beneficiary selection criteria will consider newly displaced persons, female headed households, child-headed households, the elderly in the community and persons with disabilities to ensure the most vulnerable groups are targeted.
To ensure sustainability, the ESKs will be established on lands with relatively long land agreements (three years and above). This will be ascertained through solicitation of written agreements from IDP site leaders and the subsequent confirmation of their validity from respective local authorities. ESK construction will be keen on COVID-19 and basic site planning aspects such as distance between ESKs, roads, fire breaks, drainage and distance from toilets.
Due to COVD-19, SSWC will use hotline numbers for CFRM. The anticipated data to be collected include among others both compliments and complaints: the quality of the ESKs and NFIs, fairness of beneficiary selection processes, shortness of items distributed, delays and other feedback. This will ensure that community participation and AAP is at the center of the project.
Post Distribution Monitoring (PDM) and Post construction monitoring (PCM) will be conducted after every distribution and construction respectively. The monitoring exercises will provide beneficiary feedback on the effectiveness of the distribution. 70% of the beneficiaries will take part of the exercise to ensure proper representation and that exact feelings are recorded about the processes and quality of distribution. The PDM/PCMs will also help to know the beneficiary satisfaction of the items distributed, identify the needs and feelings of the community better and inform on the effectiveness of the activities and achievements of targets while providing guidance towards success.

Provision of Integrated Support Through Protection, WASH, Shelter and CCCM Interventions in Beletxawa IDP Settlements. To improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at site level in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region to ensure equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, with a clear focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. According to HNO 2020, an estimated 709,000 new displacements were reported from January to December 2019, mostly to urban areas, where displaced people move to private IDP sites with poor living conditions and little access to basic services. There are over 2,000 recorded IDP sites across Somalia. Approximately 85 percent of the sites are informal settlements on private land and about 74 percent of them are in urban areas according to the Detailed Site Assessment (DSA). According to the DSA, over 70 percent of IDPs in informal sites lack access to information about their rights and available services. Displaced communities, especially new arrivals, people with disabilities and women need access to information and representation in the community governance structure to make informed decisions about how to receive services and potential solutions to displacement. This year (2020), Somalia has seen serious flooding which have forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes amid risks of COVID-19. According to UNHCR more than 150,000 Somalis have been forced to flee their homes since late June, including some 23,000 in the last week of July, due to flash and riverine flooding in the Southern regions of Somalia. As of 19 May (OCHA), ongoing flash and riverine flooding in Somalia has affected about 919,000 people, of whom 412,000 have been displaced and 24 killed, in 29 districts. 

The displaced people in informal sites in Banadir, Lower Shebelle, Lower Jubba, and Gedo Region are in greatest need of CCCM services to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level. The target areas have been through successive years of drought and conflict, leaving the population vulnerable to shocks and inhibiting a sustainable return to places of origin. The displaced population in these areas are living in precarious conditions with their basic needs not met due to inconsistent service provision and exclusion with all existing coordination and management mechanisms at site level being informal, with most sites managed by landlords and gatekeepers limiting accountability and adherence to minimum standards. While ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need, NoFYL will ensure to enhance the accountability of affected populations through community participation and consistent engagement with a focus on moving toward attaining durable solutions. 

NoFYL intends to scale up its CCCM program to contribute towards strengthening camp coordination and camp management to improve the living conditions and protection of IDPs at the site level by ensuring equitable access to services and assistance of all persons in need. All the project activities will be carried out to maximize community participation and enhance the accountability of humanitarian actors to the affected population. NoFYL will coordinate with relevant responders and mobilized towards providing sectorial assistance to those identified as very vulnerable at the site level. Together with the established site governance, NoFYL will carry out service monitoring activities aimed at highlighting service gaps, and ensuring that minimum standards are being adhered to at the site-level. To ensure that sites are safe and hygiene conditions are ensured NoFYL will provide training on-site maintenance and site planning to camp committees to strengthen their capacity, Support community-led site maintenance activities to ensure the upkeep of sites through cash for work activities, distribution of tools to site maintenance committees. The project will also support maintaining inter-sector complaints feedback mechanisms (CFMs) at the IDP site-level.

The project will be implemented in 4 regions, including Banaadir, Gedo region covering Beletxaawo and Ceelwaaq districts, and Lower Juba covering Kismayo. The project will target 60 sites in total targeting an estimated IDP population of 64,000 to be verified through the detailed site assessments.

In line with HRP strategic objective 1, specific objective 1.2, this project will contribute to the WASH cluster objective of delivering life-saving WASH assistance to reduce acute needs among most vulnerable settlements and communities through emergency water tracking, water vouchers, provision of hygiene kits and hygiene promotion activities. Lifesaving Wash assistance will target hard to reach communities in Garbaharey and Dolow districts and IDPs households in Banadir and Dolow. Protection Response for Vulnerable Lebanese and Other Resident Populations According to OCHA, approximately 393,000 people across 26 districts are in need of GBV services in 2022, a significant increase from 67,000 people in need in the 2021 ERP. Around a quarter of Lebanese households reported having safety and security concerns for women in their community (OCHA, 2022). The GBVIMS shows that in the last quarter of 2022, the most common types of GBV incidents were physical assault and emotional abuse mostly happening in the context of intimate partner violence, followed by forced marriage. Protection risks for all targeted populations remains high, with women and girls facing significant risks of multiple forms of GBV. The economic insecurity combined with different levels of crisis affecting the country as well as risks related to legal status, add to these vulnerabilities. Shortage in electricity and increased transportation and telecom prices all act as contributing factors to different forms of GBV in all locations. Sexual harassment through online platform and cyber abuse is an emerging GBV trend. Another alarming trend is the increased rates of sexual exploitation by landlords and employers especially affecting female heads of households with financial vulnerability.  Preventing, mitigating, and responding to GBV in emergencies is a lifesaving priority and an essential component of humanitarian action, especially in a country with extreme structural gender inequalities. 

The below proposed activities focus on survivor-centered care with case management teams working to meet the immediate, lifesaving needs of women and girls while laying the groundwork for survivors of GBV, their families and their communities to recover. Under the GBV prevention component, the project will be providing dignity kits to 3000 beneficiaries and awareness raising sessions to 2500 non-unique beneficiaries. There will be an overlap of beneficiaries attending awareness sessions and receiving dignity kits. Also, 120 men will receive men engagement activities (Cycle of Violence), and those are already counted under the awareness sessions target. The COV is composed of three sessions including: Life and daily stressors, Violence and How to deal with stressors. 
Aim of the sessions:
 During the dire economic situation in the country, the team will look at the effects of the family on this period, and its goal is the ability to mitigate its effects on both, society and family. 
 In the three sessions, the team will discuss together with the men about the stress and frustrations of the situation as well its effects on the family members and their reactions towards it in a positive or negative way.
Under the GBV response component, IMC will be providing focused PSS groups for 300 beneficiaries as well as GBV case management (including emergency cash assistance). IMC will also provide non-focused PSS for 500 unique beneficiaries (which overlap with the focused PSS activities as well as the dignity kits beneficiaries). IMC will provide the services in three safe spaces in Akkar, Beirut and South. GBV department is well established in these areas with well-trained case workers and social workers.

Based on IMC’s presence in the different areas proposed under this project, the objectives of the ERP directly address the needs of the communities especially vulnerable women and girls. IMC will organize empowerment activities for women and girls and will engage with men as allies to prevent GBV. IMC will coordinate with local actors, authorities, and other sectors to strengthen GBV prevention and response and will continue working with communities to shift social norms that contribute to GBV and threaten the protection and wellbeing of women and children.
